items.title: Embrace Your Obsessions: Susan Orlean on the Antidote to the Meaninglessness of Life
items.description: Every great book, whatever its subject or genre or style, is about one thing only: the eternal question of what gives meaning to our tiny, transient lives. And every answer given, however faintly whispered, points to one thing only: the quality of attention we pay to those lives. items.title: Legendary Cellist Pablo Casals, at Age 93, on Creative Vitality and How Working with Love Prolongs Your Life
items.description: "The man who works and is never bored is never old. Work and interest in worthwhile things are the best remedy for age."

items.title: The Art of Conversation: Timeless Do’s and Don’ts from 1866
items.description: "In disputes upon moral or scientific points, ever let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery."

items.title: The Only Three Distinctions Between People
items.description: It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos of them. Our cognitive inheritance is a restless yearning to fathom how things cohere and where they belong, a yearning we have given shape to in laws and labels, weights and balances, hierarchies and categories. items.title: How to Hear the Song of Life
items.description: “When we have learned how to listen to trees,” Hermann Hesse wrote in one of his least known, most beautiful essays, “then the brevity and the quickness and the childlike hastiness of our thoughts achieve an incomparable joy. Whoever has learned how to listen to trees no longer wants to be a tree. He wants to be nothing except what he is. That is home. items.title: J.R.R. Tolkien on Fairy Tales, Language, the Psychology of Fantasy, and Why There’s No Such Thing as Writing “For Children”
items.description: "Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else (make something new), may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds."

items.title: Love Anyway
items.description: You know that the price of life is death, that the price of love is loss, and still you watch the golden afternoon light fall on a face you love, knowing that the light will soon fade, knowing that the loving face too will one day fade to indifference or bone, and you love anyway — because life is transient but possible, because love alone bridges the impossible and the eternal. items.title: How to Criticize with Kindness: Philosopher Daniel Dennett on the Four Steps to Arguing Intelligently
items.description: "Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?"

items.title: What Makes You Yourself: Posidonia Australis, Pando, and the Paradox of Personhood
items.description: Bigger than Manhattan, Earth’s largest living organism sways in the surf south of Australia: Posidonia australis — a species of seagrass that, unable to flower, clones itself. Older than mathematics and the written word, it has been cloning itself since before the pyramids were built — a kind of immortality. items.title: Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing
items.description: "Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve… to live in the world with the absence of someone… ingrained in your understanding of the world… For the brain, [they are] simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time."

items.title: The Relief of Rock Bottom: George Orwell and the Secret Springboard of Success
items.description: It happens to everyone — to kings and paupers, to astronauts and poets. Nothing will protect you from it — not money, not love, not perfect health — for it spares no life that is fully lived, not the sunniest or the most privileged or the best planned. It begins with the wall — the one you hit over and over and over, not breaking through. And then, after the exhausted collapse, the bottom. items.title: Necessary Losses: The Life-Shaping Art of Letting Go
items.description: "We cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss. And we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and leaving and letting go."

items.title: The Four Buddhist Mantras for Turning Fear into Love
items.description: "When you love someone, the best thing you can offer that person is your presence."

items.title: Where the Joy Is
items.description: One of the most important things I have learned about life is that joy is a choice, an orientation, a practice of bending the mind in the direction of gladness — a choice increasingly countercultural in our age of competitive complaint, and yet all the more urgent precisely because our world gives us so many valid reasons for despair. “Experience of conflict and a load of suffering has taught me that what matters above all is to celebrate joy… Life is wasted when we make it more terrifying, prec

items.title: Between Psyche and Cyborg: Carl Jung’s Legacy and the Countercultural Courage to Reclaim the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age
items.description: "A reanimated world is one in which spirit and matter are not just equally regarded but recognized as mutually dependent."
